conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m the surgery doctor on call. I understand you came in with abdominal pain and bloating, plus some low blood sugars. Can you tell me what’s been going on over the last few days?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s been about four days of belly pain and feeling really swollen. I’m nauseated but not throwing up. And my sugars have been dropping a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Where is the pain—more on the right side, left, or all over? And is it constant or crampy?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Mostly lower belly and sometimes on the right. It comes and goes, like cramps, but it’s been more constant tonight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Any vomiting, fevers, chills, or trouble breathing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No fever. No vomiting. Just nausea and I feel shaky when my sugar drops.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Are you still using your G-tube feeds? Any change in the tube site or output?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Tube feeds are going in okay. The site looks fine. I’ve been trying not to eat much by mouth like nutrition told me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Are you still taking metronidazole—Flagyl—for the bacterial overgrowth?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ve been taking it. And my lactulose dose was increased last week, so I’ve been going to the bathroom more.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Any burning when you pee, urgency, or back pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Actually yes—burning and I feel like I have to go a lot, but not much comes out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thanks—that’s helpful. We’ll check labs and urine testing. We also got an abdominal X-ray to look for obstruction or free air, and we’ll likely do an ultrasound of the gallbladder since you have some right-sided pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m scared it’s another blockage. With my bypass history, it always feels like something is wrong.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s completely understandable. The good news is your exam right now doesn’t suggest an emergency, and we’re checking imaging to be safe. We’ll also keep a close eye on your blood sugars while you’re here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your abdominal X-ray is back. It shows a normal bowel gas pattern—no obstruction and no free air. It does show moderate stool in the right side of the colon, which can contribute to bloating and crampy pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s constipation? But I’ve been having more bowel movements with the lactulose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can still happen—sometimes you can have frequent stools but still have stool sitting higher up. We’ll keep your bowel regimen going and make sure you’re hydrated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my sugars? My monitor keeps going off.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked a blood sugar here and it’s okay at the moment. We’ll do frequent checks and we’re going to involve endocrinology to help with the hypoglycemia plan and your continuous glucose monitor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your morning labs are reassuring overall. One of the tests we sent, cortisol, is elevated, but that can happen with stress and illness. Nothing here suggests an acute surgical problem.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Does that mean my adrenal glands are okay? I’ve worried about that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Based on what we have, there’s no sign of adrenal insufficiency. Endocrinology can also weigh in when they see you, especially since the main issue is the low sugars after bypass.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your right upper quadrant ultrasound is back—no gallstones and no signs of gallbladder infection. Liver and bile ducts look normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s a relief. Then why does it hurt on the right sometimes?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Pain can come from bowel distention, stool burden, or chronic abdominal pain related to your prior surgeries. The key is we’re not seeing anything dangerous like obstruction or gallbladder disease today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re going to continue your tube feeds as directed. Nutrition is documenting the enteral feeding plan, and we’ll keep your oral intake limited to liquids for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Liquids only again? I’m worried I’ll crash if I don’t eat.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll balance that. The tube feeds provide steady nutrition, and for the hypoglycemia we’ll focus on responding earlier when your glucose starts trending down, rather than waiting until it alarms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your urine testing is consistent with a urinary tract infection, which can also make you feel unwell and worsen appetite and glucose swings. We’re starting an antibiotic called Bactrim by mouth.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve taken that before. How long do I need it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning a total of five days of treatment. Since you’ll start it here, you’ll go home with the remaining doses—twice a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My belly still hurts. Tylenol isn’t touching it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We can give you stronger pain medication as needed, but we’ll use the lowest effective dose and keep it short-term. Opioids can worsen constipation, so we’ll be careful and keep your bowel meds going.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Endocrinology reviewed your glucose monitor data with you. Their main concern is that you’ve been waiting for the alarm before taking sugar, which means you’re treating late.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I thought the alarm meant it was time to fix it. I didn’t want to overdo sugar and then dump.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. Their recommendation is to act earlier—when you see the number trending down—so you can take a smaller amount of sugar and prevent a bigger crash. That can actually reduce dumping-type swings.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: If it’s dropping, what should I take? I’m mostly on tube feeds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They’ll give you a specific plan, but the principle is quick sugar when it’s falling—don’t wait for the alarm. Since you’re on tube feeds, we’ll also make sure your feeding schedule is consistent and you have a way to take sugar safely if you’re symptomatic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How was the night—any vomiting, worsening pain, or very low sugars?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No vomiting. Pain is better with the meds. My sugar dipped once but I treated it earlier like they said and it didn’t get as bad.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s exactly what we want. Any urinary symptoms today—burning or urgency?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little burning still, but it’s less than yesterday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great—Bactrim often starts helping within a day or two. We’ll keep you on it and make sure you can tolerate everything by mouth or tube before discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Do I need surgery for any of this? I keep ending up back here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not based on what we’re seeing this admission. Imaging doesn’t show obstruction or gallbladder disease, and your abdomen is soft without signs of an acute surgical issue. The focus is treating the UTI, managing chronic abdominal pain, and tightening the hypoglycemia plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m worried about being on Flagyl so long. Do I keep taking it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—continue the Flagyl as you’ve been prescribed for the small bowel bacterial overgrowth. We’re not changing that plan during this stay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re starting to plan for discharge tomorrow if things stay stable: pain controlled with oral meds, sugars manageable with the new approach, and UTI improving on antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I go home with pain meds? I don’t want to be stuck in pain, but I also don’t want to get constipated again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll give a short course of an oral pain medication to use only as needed. Keep taking lactulose and bisacodyl as directed, drink the liquids you’re allowed, and call if constipation or pain worsens.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning—your vitals look good and your abdominal exam is improved: soft, only mild tenderness, not distended. Are you comfortable going home today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I think so. I’m still nervous about the low sugars at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Understandable. The key instructions are: keep trending your glucose, and when you see it dropping, take in sugar then—don’t wait for the alarm. Endocrinology also wants you to follow up with your outpatient doctor who manages your blood sugars.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the UTI—just finish the Bactrim?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. You’ll take Bactrim DS one tablet twice daily to complete five total days of treatment. If you develop fever, flank pain, or worsening urinary symptoms, you should call your primary care provider or come back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about eating? Can I have solids?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: For now, no solid food by mouth—continue liquids only, and continue tube feeds as directed. That’s to keep things steady while your symptoms settle and to help with glucose stability.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been struggling mentally with all of this. I missed my therapy appointment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad you told me. Please reschedule with your psychologist/therapist as soon as you can, and follow up with your primary care provider too. We’ll include that in your discharge instructions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Before you leave: you’re going home with Bactrim to finish the UTI treatment, a short supply of pain medication as needed, and you’ll continue Flagyl and your usual meds. Any last questions about the glucose monitor plan?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just to be clear—if I see it trending down, I treat it even if it hasn’t alarmed yet?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Treat early when it’s dropping, so you can prevent a severe low. And keep your tube feeds consistent. If you have repeated lows despite that, call your endocrinology doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Thank you for explaining it in a way I can follow. I’ll finish the antibiotics and set up my follow-ups.
